summary.text: For arbitrarily large primes \(p\), the only admissible integers up to \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\), so \(a(p)=2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), the claimed lower bound becomes \(\sqrt{\log p}\), which exceeds \(2\) for all sufficiently large such primes, giving a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ divides }n\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(P(m)\) denotes the set of prime factors of \(m\), with \(P(1)=\varnothing\), then
\[
a(n)=\#\{k:1\le k\le n,\ P(k)\subseteq P(n)\}.
\]
We disprove the asserted eventual lower bound by evaluating \(a(n)\) at prime values of \(n\).

First we establish that
\[
a(p)=2
\tag{1}
\]
for every prime \(p\). Since \(p\) is prime, its set of prime factors is exactly \(\{p\}\). Both \(k=1\) and \(k=p\) are counted: the integer \(1\) has no prime factors, while the only prime factor of \(p\) is \(p\) itself.

Conversely, suppose that \(1\le k\le p\) and that every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\). There are two cases. If \(k=1\), it is one of the two integers already listed. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has a prime divisor. Indeed, among the divisors of \(k\) greater than \(1\), choose the least one, say \(q\); if \(q\) were composite, one of its proper factors greater than \(1\) would also divide \(k\), contradicting minimality, so \(q\) is prime. By the assumed containment of prime-factor sets, this prime divisor \(q\) must equal \(p\). Thus \(p\mid k\). Since \(k\) is positive and \(k\le p\), divisibility by \(p\) forces \(k=p\). Therefore the counted set is exactly \(\{1,p\}\). As a prime is not equal to \(1\), these are distinct, proving (1).

We will also use the elementary fact that primes occur beyond every prescribed bound. For completeness, let \(M\) be a positive integer. The integer \(M!+1\) is greater than \(1\), so it has a prime divisor \(p\). If \(p\le M\), then, because \(p\) is one of the positive integers occurring among the factors of \(M!\), we would have \(p\mid M!\). But \(p\mid M!+1\) as well, and hence \(p\) would divide their difference \(1\), which is impossible for a prime. Consequently \(p>M\). Thus, in particular, one can choose a prime simultaneously larger than any given natural-number threshold and any given fixed real threshold.

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the stated conjecture were true. Thus suppose that for every real \(\epsilon>0\), there were a natural number \(N\) such that for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n),
\tag{2}
\]
where \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and the natural numbers in this real-valued inequality are regarded as real numbers.

Apply this assertion with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be some \(N\) such that
\[
(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n)
\tag{3}
\]
for every \(n\ge N\).

Choose a positive integer \(M\) larger than both \(N\) and the real number \(e^4\); such an integer exists by the Archimedean property. By the preceding Euclidean argument, there is a prime \(p>M\). In particular,
\[
p\ge N
\quad\text{and}\quad
p>e^4.
\]
The natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers, so
\[
\log p>\log(e^4)=4.
\tag{4}
\]
Because both sides are positive, taking square roots preserves this strict inequality. Hence
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>4^{1/2}=2.
\tag{5}
\]
On the other hand, \(p\ge N\), so (3), applied to \(n=p\), gives
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
By (1), \(a(p)=2\), and therefore
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le 2,
\tag{6}
\]
which directly contradicts (5).

Thus the proposed statement cannot hold. Explicitly, already for \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), every proposed threshold \(N\) is defeated by a sufficiently large prime \(p\): at that prime, \(a(p)=2\), whereas \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\). Therefore it is false that for every \(\epsilon>0\), one has
\[
a(n)\ge (\log n)^{1-\epsilon}
\]
for all sufficiently large \(n\).
